title: Charles Drew's 'Blood for Britain' Plasma Revolution, Richard Lewisohn's Citrate & Modern 1:1:1 Trauma Resuscitation — Ending Alexis Carrel's direct artery-to-vein sewing via Hustin, Agote & Richard Lewisohn's 1915 0.2% sodium citrate Ca2+ chelation, Charles Richard Drew's 1940 Columbia MedScD, 'Blood for Britain' Blitz plasma cold chain, his principled resignation over racially segregated Red Cross blood & factual debunking of the 1950 Alamance General crash myth, Vietnam's crystalloid Lethal Triad vs. PROPPR 1:1:1 (exsanguination 9.2% vs 14.6%) & CRASH-2 tranexamic acid (N=20,211), plus 0.01-Å walks inside Plasminogen Kringle 1–TXA (PDB 1CEB), Factor VIIa Gla (PDB 1DAN), Prothrombin Gla–Ca2+–LPS (PDB 1NL2) & Human Serum Albumin (PDB 1N5U).

teenKit.tldr: Before blood banks, doctors had to slice open a healthy donor's wrist and sew their artery directly into a dying patient's vein. Chemistry, logistics, and brilliant scientists changed everything to create modern life-saving trauma care.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Every time someone receives a routine blood transfusion or plasma during an emergency, they are benefiting from chemical tricks and historical breakthroughs born out of wartime desperation.
keyTakeaways: Early blood transfusions were a brutal, one-way surgical circus because blood instantly clots outside the body within five minutes.
Adding 0.2% sodium citrate stops the clotting clock by locking up calcium ions, making blood storage and banking possible for the first time.
Dr. Charles Drew revolutionized emergency medicine by creating the 'Blood for Britain' plasma cold chain during WWII, though he later resigned in protest over racist blood segregation.

vocab.meaning: A chemical salt added to blood that grabs onto calcium ions to stop the blood from clotting.
The yellowish liquid part of blood that carries cells, nutrients, and clotting factors without needing red blood cells to match types.
A dangerous medical downward spiral in trauma patients involving hypothermia, metabolic acidosis, and failing blood clotting.
A low-cost molecular drug that blocks proteins from breaking down blood clots, saving lives during severe bleeding.

quiz.question: Why did early 20th-century surgeons have to sew a donor's artery directly into a patient's vein?
options: To filter out bacteria from the blood
Because blood clotted into a useless jelly within minutes of touching glass or metal
To measure the exact blood pressure of the donor
Because plastic tubing hadn't been invented yet
quiz.explanation: Blood instantly triggers its own clotting cascade when it leaves the smooth inner lining of a blood vessel, turning solid within minutes.

quiz.question: How does sodium citrate successfully prevent blood from clotting in a storage bag?
options: It binds to calcium ions, which are required for the clotting chemical reaction to occur
It increases the oxygen levels in the plasma
quiz.explanation: Calcium acts as a vital key in the body's clotting pathway, and sodium citrate locks up that calcium so the clotting machinery cannot start.

quiz.question: What major contribution did Dr. Charles Drew make during World War II?
options: Inventing the first synthetic blood substitute
Organizing the 'Blood for Britain' plasma supply system and pioneering blood bank preservation
Performing the first direct artery-to-vein human transplant
quiz.explanation: Dr. Drew mastered the processing and large-scale shipping of plasma to save countless lives during the London Blitz.
